t:
(a) Definitions.—For the purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
        (1) Banning.—The term “Banning” means the City of Banning, which is located in Riverside County, California adjacent to the Morongo Indian Reservation. 
        (2) Fields.—The term “Fields” means Lloyd L. Fields, the owner of record of Parcel A. 
        (3) Map.—The term “map” means the map entitled ‘Morongo Indian Reservation, County of Riverside, State of California Land Exchange Map’, and dated May 22, 2014, which is on file in the Bureau of Land Management State Office in Sacramento, California. 
        (4) Parcel a.—The term “Parcel A” means the approximately 41.15 acres designated on the map as “Fields lands”. 
        (5) Parcel b.—The term “Parcel B” means the approximately 41.15 acres designated on the map as “Morongo lands”. 
        (6) Parcel c.—The term “Parcel C” means the approximately 1.21 acres designated on the map as “Banning land”. 
        (7) Parcel d.—The term “Parcel D” means the approximately 1.76 acres designated on the map as “Easement to Banning”. 
        (8) Secretary.—The term “Secretary” means the Secretary of the Interior. 
        (9) Tribe.—The term “Tribe” means the Morongo Band of Mission Indians, a federally recognized Indian tribe.  
    (b) Transfer of Lands; Trust Lands, Easement.—
        (1) Transfer of parcel a and parcel b and easement over parcel d.—Subject to any valid existing rights of any third parties and to legal review and approval of the form and content of any and all instruments of conveyance and policies of title insurance, upon receipt by the Secretary of confirmation that Fields has duly executed and deposited with a mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder in California a deed conveying clear and unencumbered title to Parcel A to the United States in trust for the exclusive use and benefit of the Tribe, and upon receipt by Fields of confirmation that the Secretary has duly executed and deposited into escrow with the same mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder a patent conveying clear and unencumbered title in fee simple to Parcel B to Fields and has duly executed and deposited into escrow with the same mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder an easement to the City for a public right-of-way over Parcel D, the Secretary shall instruct the escrow holder to simultaneously cause—
            (A) the patent to Parcel B to be recorded and issued to Fields; 
            (B) the easement over Parcel D to be recorded and issued to the City; and 
            (C) the deed to Parcel A to be delivered to the Secretary, who shall immediately cause said deed to be recorded and held in trust for the Tribe.  
        (2) Transfer of parcel c.—After the simultaneous transfer of parcels A, B, and D under paragraph (1), upon receipt by the Secretary of confirmation that the City has vacated its interest in Parcel C pursuant to all applicable State and local laws, the Secretary shall immediately cause Parcel C to be held in trust for the Tribe subject to—
            (A) any valid existing rights of any third parties; and 
            (B) legal review and approval of the form and content of any and all instruments of conveyance.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the land exchange involves outside parties (Fields, the City of Banning, the Tribe) and a "mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder", which sounds like coordination. But this is a congressionally directed property transaction: the Secretary's duties are ministerial and are triggered once the conveyance documents are deposited. Nothing requires the Secretary to consult, hold a hearing, take comments, or receive advice before making a federal decision, and no right to sue is granted.
fable.s: the Secretary shall instruct the escrow holder to simultaneously cause

opus.w: Congress itself directs this land exchange. The outside parties (Fields, the City, the Tribe) take part only as parties to the property deal, by signing deeds, using escrow and vacating interests. That is like a contract or conveyance, not consultation on a federal decision. The 'mutually acceptable' escrow holder looks like coordination with an outsider, but it is a closing detail, and the section has no comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue.
opus.s: upon receipt by the Secretary of confirmation that Fields has duly executed and deposited with a mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder in California a deed conveying clear and unencumbered title to Parcel A to the United States in trust for the exclusive use and benefit of the Tribe
opus.b:
I labelled this section **No**: it carries out a land exchange that Congress has already decided, and nobody outside the government is consulted on that decision.

**The tempting reading.** Several outside parties appear: Fields, the City of Banning and the Morongo Tribe. The Secretary must also use a "mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder." That sounds like the Secretary coordinating with outsiders before acting.

**Why it fails.** The statute itself orders the exchange. Fields and the City take part only as parties to the deal. They sign deeds, put them in escrow, give up interests and receive land or an easement. That is like signing a contract, which the definition excludes. Agreeing on an escrow holder is a detail of closing the deal, not consultation on a policy choice. The section also has no comment period, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue.

The choice of escrow holder is the closest call, so my confidence is moderate (0.72).

qwen_chat.w: This section describes a specific land exchange transaction where the Secretary's actions are conditioned on the simultaneous performance of other parties (Fields and the City) in an escrow arrangement. This is a mechanical execution of a statutory mandate, not a process of consultation, coordination, or participation in a federal decision-making process. The outside parties are not providing advice, comments, or input to influence a decision; they are fulfilling contractual/statutory obligations to complete a transfer. Therefore, it does not meet the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.s: upon receipt by the Secretary of confirmation that Fields has duly executed and deposited with a mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder in California a deed conveying clear and unencumbered title to Parcel A to the United States in trust for the exclusive use and benefit of the Tribe, and upon receipt by Fields of confirmation that the Secretary has duly executed and deposited into escrow with the same mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder a patent conveying clear and unencumbered title in fee simple to Parcel B to Fields and has duly executed and deposited into escrow with the same mutually acceptable and jointly instructed escrow holder an easement to the City for a public right-of-way over Parcel D, the Secretary shall instruct the escrow holder to simultaneously cause
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Secretary must wait for confirmation from private parties (Fields) and local governments (the City of Banning) before executing the land transfer, this constitutes "coordination" or "consultation" with outside entities. However, this is a conditional execution of a specific statutory mandate (a land exchange), not a process where the government seeks input, advice, or approval from outsiders to *make* a policy decision. The outside parties are simply fulfilling their side of a pre-negotiated deal defined by Congress. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits or grants, and this is analogous to a transactional requirement rather than participatory decision-making. Furthermore, the "coordination" is strictly mechanical (escrow instructions) rather than deliberative.
